notes:
Task and constraints: Given a non-empty integer array where every value occurs twice except one, return the unpaired value. The statement requires linear time and constant extra space.
Idea: Sorts nums in place, then walks in pairs. Equal neighbors are skipped together; the first unequal pair identifies the single value, or the last value is returned if all earlier pairs matched.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting followed by adjacent-pair scanning groups equal values together, so paired occurrences can be skipped.
Invariant: At each loop iteration, all positions before i have been consumed as equal pairs.
Edge cases: A one-element array reaches nums[-1]. Negative values sort normally. This code is correct for the stated pairing rule but violates the required linear runtime because it sorts.
Complexity: Time is O(n log n) for sorting plus O(n) scanning; auxiliary sorting space depends on Python's sort implementation, so constant extra space is not established.

Task and constraints: Given a non-empty integer array where every value occurs twice except one, return the value occurring once, with linear runtime and constant extra space.
Idea: reduce applies bitwise XOR to every array element, combining them into one result.
Technique and why it applies: Bitwise XOR is appropriate because x XOR x is zero and zero XOR x is x; paired values cancel regardless of order.
Invariant: After each reduction step, the accumulator is the XOR of all elements processed so far.
Edge cases: A single value returns itself. Negative integers work with Python's integer XOR semantics; the input array is not modified.
Complexity: Time is O(n), since each value is combined once; auxiliary space is O(1) for the reduction accumulator.

Task and constraints: Every integer occurs three times except one occurring once; return that value in linear time and constant extra space.
Idea: Computes the total sum, pops all values from nums into a set, and returns (three times the set sum minus the original total) divided by two.
Technique and why it applies: Set-based sum arithmetic isolates the singleton because repeated values contribute three times to the total but once to the unique-value sum.
Invariant: Before mutation, total records the original sum; after the loop, uniqueTotals contains every distinct input value.
Edge cases: The code empties the caller's nums list. Python's / returns a float, not an integer, so the return type can violate the requested integer result; the method also fails the constant-extra-space requirement.
Complexity: Expected time is O(n) for set insertion and summation; extra space is O(n) for the set, and the author provides no complexity label.

Task and constraints: Determine whether s can be segmented into one or more dictionary words, allowing a word to be reused.
Idea: Recursively tests whether the remaining target can be constructed. It tries each dictionary word matching the target prefix and succeeds if any resulting suffix can be constructed; results are memoized by suffix string.
Technique and why it applies: Memoized recursion explores word-boundary choices while reusing answers for identical suffixes.
Invariant: A true memo entry means that suffix has a valid segmentation; a false entry means every dictionary-word prefix tried failed.
Edge cases: The empty suffix is the successful base case. If no word matches the next prefix, the suffix is memoized false. Substring slicing creates new strings.
Complexity: With memoization there are at most O(n) distinct suffix states, each scanning the dictionary and doing prefix/slice work; time is roughly O(n*D*L), where D is dictionary size and L the compared word length, and memo storage can be O(n²) in copied suffix characters.

Task and constraints: Determine whether s can be segmented into dictionary words, with words reusable and lowercase input strings.
Idea: Builds a boolean array where can_break[i] says whether the first i characters can be segmented. For each endpoint it tries suffix lengths up to the longest dictionary word.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix dynamic programming works because a valid segmentation ending at i consists of a valid earlier prefix followed by one dictionary word.
Invariant: Before processing endpoint i, can_break[j] is correct for every prefix length j less than i.
Edge cases: can_break[0] is true for the empty prefix. A word longer than the examined maximum length is never considered; list membership is used for dictionary lookup.
Complexity: The author labels time O(n*l²) and space O(n). The code has O(n*l) candidate substrings, but `in wordDict` scans a list and substring slicing costs up to O(l), so the label can be accurate for bounded dictionary-search assumptions but is not a complete bound when dictionary size is counted; DP storage is O(n).

Task and constraints: Return every sentence formed by splitting s into dictionary words, with words reusable and any output order accepted.
Idea: Groups dictionary words by their first character. Recursion tries words in the matching group, appends a matching word to the path, explores the remaining suffix, then removes that word.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking enumerates all valid word-boundary choices, while first-character grouping avoids testing words that cannot start at the current position.
Invariant: ans contains the words chosen for the consumed prefix of s; every recursive call advances idx by the length of a matched word.
Edge cases: If no word matches at an index, that branch returns no sentence. The code relies on defaultdict being imported elsewhere; as shown, it raises NameError if that import is absent.
Complexity: Runtime depends on the number and total length of valid sentences and can be exponential in s; recursion depth is O(n), with O(n) path state plus output storage.

Task and constraints: Return all valid dictionary-word sentences that concatenate to s, allowing reuse of dictionary words.
Idea: First computes whether each prefix can break and records valid dictionary substrings in a two-dimensional table. If the whole string is breakable, a helper recursively enumerates paths through valid substrings.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix DP prunes impossible sentences, and backtracking reconstructs every valid segmentation from the stored substring choices.
Invariant: valid[i][j] marks a dictionary word exactly when that substring was found during the DP; the helper path spells the already-consumed prefix.
Edge cases: If the whole string cannot break, it returns an empty list without enumeration. Repeated choices may produce many sentences, and `path += [...]` temporarily creates a new list before the recursive call.
Complexity: The author labels space O(n²), consistent with the valid-substring table, though output and recursive paths add more. Time includes O(n²) preprocessing plus work proportional to all generated sentences and their lengths.

Task and constraints: Given unique points on a plane, return the maximum number lying on one straight line; there are at most 300 points.
Idea: For each anchor point, counts the slope to every other point in a dictionary and uses the largest slope count plus one as the line size.
Technique and why it applies: Anchor-based slope counting groups points that share a line through the chosen anchor.
Invariant: For the current anchor, each dictionary count equals the number of other points assigned to that computed slope.
Edge cases: A one-point input returns one. Vertical lines use infinity, but horizontal lines are also assigned infinity because the code sets that value when the y difference is zero; consequently horizontal and vertical slopes collide and results can be wrong.
Complexity: Time is O(n²) expected for the nested loops and hash counts; auxiliary space is O(n) for one anchor's slope map. Floating-point slope keys may also be imprecise for some ratios.

Task and constraints: Evaluate a valid Reverse Polish Notation expression using +, -, *, and /; integer division must truncate toward zero.
Idea: Pushes integer operands onto a stack. For each operator it combines the top two values, leaves the result on the stack, and finally returns the last value.
Technique and why it applies: A stack evaluates postfix expressions because an operator consumes the two most recent operand results.
Invariant: After each token, the stack contains the intermediate values for the processed expression fragments that are not yet combined.
Edge cases: The statement guarantees valid expressions and no division by zero. `int(a / b)` truncates toward zero but first converts to floating point, which can lose precision for sufficiently large intermediate values.
Complexity: Time is O(n), since each token is processed once; stack space is O(n) in the worst case.

Task and constraints: Reverse the order of words in a string, collapsing repeated spaces and removing leading and trailing spaces.
Idea: `split()` extracts nonempty whitespace-separated words, `reversed()` reverses their order, and `join()` joins them with one space.
Technique and why it applies: Tokenization followed by reversal directly matches the requested word-order transformation.
Invariant: The reversed iterator emits exactly the original words in reverse order; joining introduces exactly one separator between adjacent words.
Edge cases: Leading, trailing, and repeated spaces are removed. The input is immutable and is not modified in place, so this does not meet the follow-up's in-place goal.
Complexity: The author labels time O(n) and space O(n), consistent with splitting into word strings and constructing the returned string.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum product of a non-empty contiguous subarray; the answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
Idea: Multiplies a running product from left to right and from right to left, updates the best product after each multiplication, and resets a running product to one at zero.
Technique and why it applies: Two directional product scans help capture a maximum product when negative values change the sign of a product.
Invariant: Within each zero-free scan segment, prod is the product of the scanned segment suffix or prefix, and maxprod is the best product seen so far.
Edge cases: Zeros split possible subarrays and are evaluated before resetting. A nonempty input is guaranteed. The input is not changed.
Complexity: Time is O(n) across two passes and auxiliary space is O(1), using only running products and indices.

Task and constraints: Return the largest product of a non-empty contiguous subarray, including arrays with negative numbers and zeros.
Idea: Maintains local maximum and minimum products. For each value, it extends a previous product or starts at the value, swapping the roles of maximum and minimum when multiplication by a negative value flips signs.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming keeps both extrema because a negative factor can turn the smallest product into the largest.
Invariant: local_max and local_min represent the maximum and minimum products ending at the current position under this code's update rules.
Edge cases: Zero resets the useful product through the `max(1, local_max)` step on the next iteration. A one-element array returns that element. The exact simultaneous assignment uses old local values.
Complexity: Time is O(n) and auxiliary space O(1), since each number updates a fixed number of scalar states.

Task and constraints: Return the largest product of a non-empty contiguous subarray, with zeros and negative values allowed.
Idea: For each value, sets local_max to the maximum of the value and the two previous extrema multiplied by it, and similarly sets local_min to their minimum; global_max records the best.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming tracks both maximum and minimum products ending at each position because multiplying by a negative can reverse their order.
Invariant: After processing an element, local_max and local_min are intended to be the extrema of products ending at that element, and global_max is the best local maximum seen.
Edge cases: The tuple assignment evaluates its right-hand side using the old values, so both calculations use the previous extrema. A zero can reset both extrema to zero for that position.
Complexity: The author labels time O(n) and space O(1), matching a single pass with three scalar values.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum in a rotated ascending array of unique integers; the required algorithm is O(log n).
Idea: Returns the first element if the array has one value or is already increasing. Otherwise it binary-searches for a drop where nums[mid-1] exceeds nums[mid], moving toward the unsorted side.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search narrows the location of the rotation boundary because the values are unique and each side is sorted.
Invariant: The minimum remains in the current search interval unless the method returns it at the detected adjacent drop.
Edge cases: A one-element array and an unrotated array are handled up front. The code has no final return after the loop, though valid stated inputs should reach a return inside the loop.
Complexity: Time is O(log n) and auxiliary space O(1), because each iteration halves the search interval and stores only indices.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum in a rotated sorted array that may contain duplicates, while reducing operations as much as possible.
Idea: Calls Python's built-in min on the entire array and returns the smallest value.
Technique and why it applies: A full scan is a direct correct baseline for finding a minimum, regardless of rotation or duplicates.
Invariant: As min scans values, the current best is the smallest value encountered so far.
Edge cases: Duplicates do not affect correctness; the constraints guarantee a nonempty array. This code ignores the opportunity to use a modified binary search and therefore does not optimize operations.
Complexity: Time is O(n), because every element may be inspected; auxiliary space is O(1) for the running minimum.

Task and constraints: Return an index of any element strictly greater than its neighbors, treating positions outside the array as negative infinity; the required runtime is O(log n).
Idea: Adds sentinel values to both ends, binary-searches for an element larger than both neighbors, and returns its index adjusted for the left sentinel.
Technique and why it applies: Binary search follows an uphill direction: if nums[m] is smaller than its right neighbor, a peak exists to the right; otherwise it searches left.
Invariant: The chosen interval continues to contain a peak under the no-equal-adjacent-values constraint.
Edge cases: A one-element array is surrounded by sentinels and returns index zero. The sentinel -2**32 is below every allowed 32-bit input value, so it behaves as negative infinity for these constraints.
Complexity: Time is O(log n) and auxiliary space is O(n) because concatenating the sentinel list copies nums into a new list, despite the logarithmic search itself using constant state.

Task and constraints: Return the largest gap between consecutive values in sorted order, using linear time and linear extra space; fewer than two values should return zero.
Idea: Finds the longest decimal digit count, converts values to zero-padded strings, applies stable counting-sort passes from the last digit to the first, then scans adjacent sorted values for the largest difference.
Technique and why it applies: Least-significant-digit radix sorting orders nonnegative integers by processing each decimal position with counting buckets.
Invariant: After each digit pass, nums is ordered by the processed suffix of digits; after all passes it is fully sorted numerically.
Edge cases: A single-element array returns zero. Inputs are nonnegative, so decimal strings need no sign handling. The method mutates values into strings and then rebinds nums to a sorted list, so the original list may contain strings after mutation.
Complexity: Time is O(n*k), where k is the maximum decimal digit count (at most 10 under the constraints), so it is linear for these bounded integers. Space is O(n*k) for string values and buckets, not strictly O(n) words if string lengths are counted.

Task and constraints: Compare two valid dotted version strings, treating missing revisions as zero and ignoring leading zeros by comparing integer values.
Idea: Splits each version at dots, converts revisions to integers, then compares aligned revision pairs, filling missing positions with zero.
Technique and why it applies: Component-wise comparison follows version ordering because the first unequal revision determines the result.
Invariant: All revision pairs before the current pair have been equal; the first difference returns -1 or 1 immediately.
Edge cases: Extra trailing zero revisions compare equal. The code converts strings to integers, which is allowed by this statement, and relies on zip_longest being imported elsewhere; without that import it raises NameError.
Complexity: Time is O(n+m) for splitting, integer conversion and pairwise comparison; space is O(n+m) for the revision lists.

Task and constraints: Convert a nonzero-denominator fraction to a decimal string, placing parentheses around a repeating fractional part.
Idea: Computes sign and integer quotient, then repeatedly multiplies the remainder by ten to produce digits while recording the positions associated with remainders; a repeated remainder identifies the cycle.
Technique and why it applies: Remainder tracking detects repetition in long division, since the same remainder produces the same future digits.
Invariant: Each stored digit is the next decimal digit from long division, and the index map records the position associated with a remainder-related value.
Edge cases: Exact divisions return the integer part. Negative signs are handled from the product of numerator and denominator. The loop keys on 10*numerator rather than the remainder itself, making the indexing logic unusual and deserving careful testing on terminating and repeating fractions.
Complexity: Time and space are O(L), where L is the number of generated decimal digits before termination or a repeated state; the statement guarantees the output length is below 10^4.

Task and constraints: Find two distinct positions in a sorted, non-decreasing array whose values sum to target; return 1-based indices and use constant extra space.
Idea: Starts pointers at both ends. If their sum is too small it moves the left pointer right; if too large it moves the right pointer left; on equality it returns the converted indices.
Technique and why it applies: Two pointers exploit sorted order: moving the left pointer increases the sum, while moving the right pointer decreases it.
Invariant: If a solution remains, at least one valid pair is inside the current pointer interval after each discarded endpoint.
Edge cases: Negative values and duplicate values are supported. The statement guarantees exactly one solution, so the loop returns a pair before pointers cross.
Complexity: Time is O(n), since each pointer moves inward at most n times; auxiliary space is O(1), aside from the two-element result.
